title: Writing a workflow

story: Thursday, 11:00. You approved Nova's plan, and Nova is building the "No projects yet" card on a VM. In the orchestrator, one activity called workInSandbox started Nova's harness, the program that runs Nova on the VM, and now it follows the build until it is done, which takes about 70 minutes.

At 11:20 someone deploys the orchestrator, and the worker process that was running workInSandbox is stopped. Nova keeps working on the VM, but nothing is following it any more, so Temporal has to notice that and start a new attempt. If the only timeout on the activity is 7 days, Temporal waits 7 days before it notices. If the timeout is 5 minutes, like a call to Jira, Temporal ends every build after 5 minutes, long before it is done.
hook.question: How does Temporal notice within two minutes that the worker of a long activity died, without putting a time limit on Nova's work?

p: A workflow never calls an activity directly. It calls a stand-in from proxyActivities, and the options you give proxyActivities decide what Temporal does when the activity is slow or fails. Each time the activity's code runs is one attempt. When an attempt fails or runs out of time, Temporal waits a little and starts a new attempt. By default it tries forever, waiting 1 second, then 2, then 4 and so on, up to 100 seconds between attempts. That rule is the activity's retry policy.

The SDK insists on a timeout, and the usual one is startToCloseTimeout: the longest a single attempt may run before Temporal ends it and retries. For a call to Jira, 5 minutes is plenty. If Jira has not answered by then, something is wrong, and a fresh attempt is the right answer. Our platform keeps these options in one file with two presets, so every workflow treats the same kind of call the same way.

notes.text: SHORT: an attempt that has not finished after 5 minutes is ended and retried.
LONG: the 7 days is never a limit on Nova's work, and the 2-minute heartbeat is what notices a dead worker. The next two sections explain both.
Workflows call act.workInSandbox(...) or peopleApis.postToSlack(...), and the options come with the stand-in.

deeper.h: Go deeper: a retry policy per kind of call
p: The default retry policy fits most calls, but not all. AWS may throttle us for a few seconds, so its calls start retrying after 1 second and stop after 10 attempts. Jira, Slack and GitHub can be down for an hour, so their calls wait longer between attempts and never stop trying; a separate rule pauses the ticket during a long outage. A wait that grows after each failure like this is called back-off.

Some errors must never be retried, because they are decisions, not accidents. If a person pressed Stop, a retry would ignore that person. An activity marks such an error with a type, for example StoppedByPerson, and the retry policy lists those types as non-retryable, so the error goes straight back to the workflow.

read.h: A heartbeat says: I am still here
p: A 70-minute build cannot work with a 5-minute timeout, and a 7-day timeout alone would mean that nobody notices a dead worker for a week. The answer is a heartbeat: a small message the activity sends to Temporal again and again while it works, which means "this attempt is alive". You also set heartbeatTimeout, the longest gap allowed between two heartbeats. If the gap grows longer, for example because the worker was killed during a deploy, Temporal ends that attempt and starts a new one on any worker that listens on the queue.

A heartbeat can carry details, such as how far the work got. The next attempt reads them from activityInfo().heartbeatDetails and continues from there instead of starting over. Here is the activity from the lab: a build of 20 steps of one second each.

Look closely at the output below. The worker died right after step 9, but attempt 2 continued after step 8. To save network traffic, the SDK sends a heartbeat at most once every 80% of heartbeatTimeout and drops the ones in between, so the last details that reached Temporal said 8. A retry can therefore repeat a little work, and that is why every step must be safe to do twice.

notes.text: attempt counts from 1. heartbeatDetails holds what the previous attempt last reported, or nothing on attempt 1.
On attempt 1 there are no details, so the build starts at step 1.
Proof of life and progress in one call. Calling it often is fine, because the SDK sends only some of the calls.

read.see:
attempt 1: building RH-1234, starting after step 0
  step 1 done
  …
  step 9 done          ← the worker is killed here
attempt 2: building RH-1234, starting after step 8
  step 9 done
  …
  step 20 done

read.h: Seven days is a safety net, not a work limit
p: Now the real activity. workInSandbox does not do Nova's work itself. It starts the harness on the VM, and from then on it only follows it. Nova runs on the VM as a system service, so killing the orchestrator's worker does not touch Nova at all.

That makes a retry harmless. When the worker dies at 11:20, its heartbeats stop, and two minutes later Temporal starts attempt 2 on a worker from the new deploy. Attempt 2 first checks whether the harness is already running on the VM. It is, so it does not start a second Nova; it re-attaches, which means it simply follows the same harness again. Nova never notices the deploy.

The 7 days still has to be there, because the SDK requires a timeout. If it ever passed, the same thing would happen: a new attempt, which re-attaches. So no timeout in Temporal limits how long Nova may work. The timeouts only notice workers that died.

notes.text: The key line for retries: attempt 2 finds the harness from attempt 1 and does not start it again.
The harness reports every 30 seconds to the broker, our service that holds the GitHub, Jira and Slack keys and makes those calls for runs. This line reads the last report.
The activity's own heartbeat to Temporal. If this worker dies, these stop, and after 2 minutes Temporal retries.
The activity returns when Nova stops for a reason: the work is done, it has a question, the VM is being taken back, or it failed.
A different problem: the VM itself went silent. Retrying cannot help, so the workflow gets the error and replaces the VM.

deeper.h: Go deeper: two heartbeats, and always giving the VM back
p: There are two heartbeats in this picture, and they answer different questions. The harness sends one to the broker every 30 seconds, which answers "is the VM alive?". After 5 minutes of silence the activity throws SandboxDead, and the workflow takes a fresh VM from the last checkpoint; a later lesson covers that recovery. The activity sends the other to Temporal, which answers "is the worker that follows the VM alive?". After 2 minutes of silence Temporal retries the activity.

The workflow also makes sure every VM it claimed is released, whatever happens. It calls releaseSandbox in a finally block, inside CancellationScope.nonCancellable, because a run that a person stops is cancelled, and a cancelled workflow could not otherwise start a new activity. releaseSandbox accepts a VM that is already gone, so calling it twice is harmless.

lab.title: Kill the worker in the middle of a long activity
needs: The p7-1 lab folder, for worker.mjs and start.mjs
lab.goal: Give a long activity a heartbeat, kill its worker in the middle, and see Temporal start a new attempt that continues from the last reported step.

guess.q: The build activity has startToCloseTimeout '7 days' and heartbeatTimeout '5 seconds'. You kill the worker at step 9 and start it again right away. What happens next?

options.text: Nothing for 7 days, because the attempt is still inside its timeout.
options.why: The heartbeat timeout fires first. 5 seconds without a heartbeat is enough for Temporal to end the attempt.

options.text: About 5 seconds after the last heartbeat, attempt 2 starts on the new worker and continues near step 9.
options.why: The heartbeats stop, Temporal ends the attempt after the heartbeat timeout, and attempt 2 reads the last reported step from the heartbeat details.

options.text: The new worker starts the build again at once, from step 1.
options.why: The service still thinks attempt 1 is running until the heartbeat timeout passes. And attempt 2 continues from the details, not from step 1.

follow.say: Keep the dev server from the last lab running, or start it again in the first tab.
follow.see:
Temporal Server:      localhost:7233
Temporal UI:          http://localhost:8233

follow.say: In a second tab, make the lab folder. Install the packages again, this time with the activity package too, and borrow the worker and the client from p7-1.

follow.see: added 150 packages, and audited 151 packages in 9s

follow.say: Write the build activity. It does 20 steps of one second, prints each one and sends a heartbeat with the step number.
Write the workflow. The 7 days is the safety net; the 5-second heartbeat timeout is the part that notices a dead worker.
Start the worker in the second tab, then start a run in a third tab and watch the steps arrive.

# third tab
cd ~/academy-labs/p7-2 && node start.mjs

follow.say: Around step 8, kill the worker hard from the third tab. Do not use Ctrl+C: it lets the worker shut down politely, and a crash or a deploy does not.

follow.say: Ask Temporal about the run. Do it twice, a few seconds apart, and compare the pending activity: attempt 1 is ended after 5 seconds of silence, and attempt 2 waits for a worker.

lab.build: Write a second long activity, runChecks(ticket), that runs the 10 checks of the QA plan, one per second. It prints "check <n> passed", sends a heartbeat with the number of the last passed check, and on a retry continues after the last reported check. Call it in the workflow after build and return both results. Restart the worker, start a run for RH-1235, kill the worker while the checks run, and start it again.
checks: After the hard kill, temporal workflow describe shows Attempt 2 and a LastFailure that says activity Heartbeat timeout.
The restarted worker prints "attempt 2: building RH-1234, starting after step N", where N is a few steps or less below where the worker died.
temporal workflow result -w nova:RH-1234 shows Status COMPLETED and "built RH-1234 in 20 steps".
For your build: the worker prints "attempt 2: checking RH-1235, starting after check N" with N above 0, and the result ends with "10 of 10 checks passed".
lab.fix: A teammate found the 7-day timeout scary and wrote "a build should be quick", so they changed the workflow's options to startToCloseTimeout: '10 seconds' and removed heartbeatTimeout. Make that change, restart the worker and start a run for RH-1300. The 20-second build never finishes in one attempt: the worker prints attempt 2, attempt 3, attempt 4, and temporal workflow describe -w nova:RH-1300 shows a LastFailure of activity StartToClose timeout. That is a time limit on the work, the thing our platform never allows. Put the safety net and the heartbeat back, then stop the old run with temporal workflow terminate -w nova:RH-1300.
explain: Why does a 7-day startToCloseTimeout never stop Nova's work, even when a build runs for 8 days?
After the hard kill, why did attempt 2 not start the moment you started the worker again?
Attempt 2 repeated a step that attempt 1 had already done. Why, and what does it mean for how you write each step?
lab.done: A run survived a hard kill of its worker in the middle of a long activity, the new attempt continued near the last reported step, and you stopped the worker and the dev server.

check.q: workInSandbox follows a 70-minute build. Which options fit it?

options.text: startToCloseTimeout: '5 minutes', like every other call
options.why: Every attempt would be ended after 5 minutes and retried, so the build could never finish in one attempt. That is a time limit on the work.
The heartbeat notices a dead worker within 2 minutes, and the 7 days is only the timeout the SDK requires. A retry re-attaches either way.
A worker that dies at minute 20 would not be noticed for almost 7 days, and the run would look busy the whole time.

check.q: The orchestrator is deployed while Nova builds, and attempt 2 of workInSandbox starts on a new worker. Why doesn't a second Nova start on the VM?

options.text: Temporal kills the harness when the first attempt ends
options.why: Temporal knows nothing about the VM. It only ends the attempt in its own records.

options.text: Temporal sends attempt 2 to the same worker process
options.why: That worker is gone. Attempt 2 runs on any worker that listens on the queue.

options.text: workInSandbox first checks whether the harness is already running, and only follows it if it is
options.why: That check makes the activity safe to run twice. A retry re-attaches to the running harness instead of starting another agent.

check.q: The build heartbeats after every step. The worker dies just after step 9, and attempt 2 says "starting after step 8". What happened?

options.text: The SDK sends only some heartbeats, so the last details Temporal received were from step 8
options.why: Heartbeats are sent at most every 80% of the heartbeat timeout. A retry may repeat a little work, so each step must be safe to do twice.

options.text: Temporal always goes back one step, to be safe
options.why: Temporal gives attempt 2 exactly the last details it received. It does not adjust them.

options.text: Step 9 failed, so Temporal removed it from the details
options.why: Nothing failed inside the step. The worker was killed before the heartbeat for step 9 was sent.

p: Every activity in the orchestrator gets its options from one file, policies.ts. SHORT, 5 minutes, is for calls to Jira, Slack, GitHub and AWS. LONG is 7 days with a 2-minute heartbeat, for workInSandbox and anything else that follows a VM. Each kind of call also has its own retry policy, and errors that are decisions, such as StoppedByPerson or ScopeDenied, are never retried.

workInSandbox starts the harness as a systemd unit over SSM, not as a long SSM command, because SSM commands end after 48 hours at most and runs have no time limit. On a retry it re-attaches to that unit. The orchestrator can therefore be deployed at any time, even while several agents are in the middle of their builds.

tickets.why: The SHORT and LONG presets, the retry policy per kind of call and the never-retry error types.
workInSandbox: start the harness once, follow it with heartbeats, re-attach on a retry.
ticketToPr calls the sandbox activities with LONG and always releases the VM in finally.

words.plain: One run of an activity's code. A retry is a new attempt of the same activity.
The rule for retries: how long to wait between attempts, and when to stop.
The longest one attempt may run before Temporal ends it and retries.
A small message a running activity sends to say it is alive, often with its progress.
The longest gap allowed between two heartbeats before Temporal ends the attempt.
A new attempt following work that is already running, instead of starting it again.

review.q: Write the two presets from policies.ts from memory, and say what each is for.
review.a: SHORT: startToCloseTimeout 5 minutes, for calls to Jira, Slack, GitHub and AWS. LONG: startToCloseTimeout 7 days and heartbeatTimeout 2 minutes, for activities that follow a VM.

review.q: A teammate asks for a 2-hour startToCloseTimeout on workInSandbox "so runaway agents stop". What do you answer?
review.a: That is a time limit on the work, which the platform never uses; the timeout would only cause a retry that re-attaches anyway. Dead workers are caught by the heartbeat, and runaway agents by the progress watcher and the cost backstop.

review.q: Why must a long activity be safe to run twice?
review.a: Retries happen after crashes and deploys, and heartbeat details can be a little behind, so a new attempt may repeat work. workInSandbox checks for a running harness before it starts one.

remember: A long activity sends heartbeats so a dead worker is noticed in minutes; its long timeout is only a safety net, and a retry re-attaches to the work.
